Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery. Physical affection such as hugs is difficult to connect to robbery-related threat activation without any supporting appraisal, memory, or strategy content, and it conflicts with the otherwise stranger/sudden-movement threat profile. Crash imagery is more characteristic of road traffic trauma than robbery and lacks any plausible link to the reported threat items.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger item about cars being hit in an accident is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of mugging/robbery. The other trigger and threat items coherently suggest interpersonal danger and hypervigilance around strangers/crowding, but crash imagery points to a motor vehicle trauma theme that is not reflected elsewhere in the profile or in the cognitive formulation. This is more than unusual; it appears to reference a different trauma context.

vignette:
Rajesh was sixty-eight when it happened, though the memory never settles into a single year – it exists in the sharp, recurring sensations that have no date. He had been finishing a late wiring job in a basement unit of a residential building, working alone after the tenants had gone to sleep. As he stepped out onto the empty side street, a man emerged from behind a dumpster, reeking of cheap whiskey and stale sweat. Rajesh remembered the smell before he remembered the voice – a rough, slurred demand for his wallet. There was no time to react. The man shoved him hard against the brick wall, one hand clamping over Rajesh’s mouth, the other pressing something cold and metallic into his ribs. He handed over his wallet, his tools, his watch. The man fled. Rajesh crouched there for what felt like hours, trembling, unable to stand, the sour odor clinging to his clothes and his skin.

In the weeks that followed, he told himself it was over. He was unharmed, after all. But his sleep began to fracture. He would wake gasping, his heart hammering, the smell of whiskey so vivid in his nostrils that he would stumble out of bed and check the locks on every door, certain someone was inside the house. His wife, Priya, would find him standing in the darkened hallway, whispering that he was fine, just a dream. But the dreams never stayed in the bed – they followed him into the morning, a lingering dread he could not shake. He began to notice that the feeling of safety he had always taken for granted during the day evaporated as soon as dusk settled. At night, even the creak of the house settling made him freeze, his breath shallow, his eyes fixed on the shadow of a curtain.

Rajesh still worked as an electrician, but he stopped accepting jobs that required evening hours. He told his boss his knees were too old for night work, but the real reason was simpler: he could not bear the walk back to his car after dark. He started leaving early, avoiding the crowded bus stops where people bumped into him without apology. Crowds became unbearable. The press of bodies at the market or the hardware store made his chest tighten – he was certain any of those strangers could be the one who would lunge at him, demand something, press something hard against his ribs. He found himself scanning every face that turned his way, reading threat into a glance that lingered half a second too long. Priya noticed that he no longer greeted neighbors on their walks. He would cross the street when someone approached, especially if they were walking quickly or made a sudden movement – a hand reaching for a phone, a child darting across the path – because his body reacted before his mind could catch up, jerking sideways, fists clenching.

The alcohol smell was the worst. Once, at a family gathering, a cousin’s husband handed him a glass of wine, and the odor that rose from the glass sent a wave of nausea through him. He set it down without drinking, excused himself to the bathroom, and stood gripping the sink for several minutes, his reflection pale and unfamiliar. He had come to believe that the world had become a series of ambushes waiting for him to let his guard down. He could not explain it to Priya – she thought he was just getting older, more irritable, more set in his ways. She urged him to see a doctor for his nerves, but he resisted, convinced that talking about it would only make it worse.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was not an argument with Priya, but a moment in the crowded aisle of a supermarket. A stranger reached past him for a box of cereal, and Rajesh swung around, his arm raised, before he even understood what he was doing. The man stepped back, startled, and Rajesh stood frozen in the fluorescent light, the smell of cleaning products mingling with the phantom trace of whiskey. He left the cart where it was and walked out. That night, he told Priya he needed to see someone. He is not sure what he hopes for – perhaps only to sleep through one night without waking, or to walk down a street without watching every shadow. But he is afraid, too, that the man behind the dumpster will never really leave.
